paraphrase: Lollaṭa's view: rasa is the stable emotion intensified (upacita) by the determinants and the rest; it exists primarily in the character imitated (Rāma) and secondarily in the actor, because of the imitation.

paraphrase: Śaṅkuka's view: rasa is the stable emotion inferred in the actor from artificially produced determinants and consequents; the actor is apprehended as Rāma as a painted horse is apprehended as a horse — a cognition neither true, false, doubtful nor similar; rasa is an 'imitation' of the stable emotion.
notes: Reported by Abhinavagupta (Abhinavabhāratī on NŚ 6), who criticises it; the author's own work is lost.

paraphrase: Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka's view: rasa is neither perceived, produced nor manifested; poetic language has, besides denotation, the power of 'making present' (bhāvakatva), which generalizes the determinants, and the power of 'making enjoyable' (bhojakatva), by which the rasa is enjoyed in a state of repose in one's own consciousness pervaded by sattva, akin to the tasting of the supreme Brahman.
notes: Reported by Abhinavagupta (Abhinavabhāratī on NŚ 6), who criticises it; the author's own work is lost. Abhinava accepts the generalization and the likeness to Brahman-tasting but rejects the two extra powers.

paraphrase: Abhinavagupta's own view: rasa is not produced, inferred or merely enjoyed through special powers; it is manifested (suggested) and relished (carvaṇā). The stable emotion, already present as a latent impression in the sensitive spectator (sahṛdaya), is awakened by generalized (sādhāraṇīkṛta) determinants, freed from the limits of 'mine' and 'another's', time and place; its relish, lasting only as long as the relishing, is a supermundane (alaukika) wonder (camatkāra) in which consciousness rests in itself (viśrānti).
notes: Paraphrase of the commentary on the rasa-sūtra, from memory.

paraphrase: Rasa arises when the obstacles (vighna) to relish are removed; there are seven: lack of credibility; being caught in the particular time and place of oneself or another; being overwhelmed by one's own pleasure or pain; lack of the means of perception; lack of clarity; the non-predominance (of the stable emotion); and doubt. The theatre's devices — preliminaries, music, conventions — serve to remove them.

paraphrase: On śānta: its stable emotion is knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), which is the self (ātman) itself, pure and free of all other feelings; it underlies every other emotion as the thread under the gems, so that love and the rest become its transient states; its goal is liberation, the highest aim of man. paraphrase: The centres of the body: the four-petalled ādhāra between anus and genitals, seat of kuṇḍalinī, the power of Brahman, which, straightened up to the brahmarandhra, bestows nectar; the six-petalled svādhiṣṭhāna at the root of the genitals; the ten-petalled maṇipūra at the navel; the twelve-petalled anāhata in the heart, place of worship of Śiva in the form of the praṇava; the sixteen-petalled viśuddhi in the throat, seat of Bhāratī (speech), whose petals bear the praṇava, the udgītha, huṃ-phaṭ, vaṣaṭ, svadhā, svāhā, namaḥ, amṛta, the seven notes and poison; the twelve-petalled lalanā at the uvula; the three-petalled ājñā between the brows; the six-petalled centre of mind; the sixteen-petalled centre of the moon with sixteen kalās (compassion, forbearance, uprightness, fortitude, dispassion and the rest); and the thousand-petalled lotus in the brahmarandhra, holding nectar that nourishes the body. When the jīva rests on each petal a particular state of mind arises.

paraphrase: In this body, covered with the accumulation of impurities, the wise attain enjoyment and liberation by the right means: enjoyment from meditation on the qualified, liberation from the unqualified. But meditation, attainable only by one-pointed mind, is not easy for men; therefore here the easy means is the glorious unstruck nāda, which sages worship by the path taught by the guru. That too, lacking charm (rakti), does not delight the minds of people; therefore (we shall describe) the struck nāda, which, extending all that is to be sung through the śrutis and the rest, delights the world and breaks worldly existence (bhava-bhañjana).

paraphrase: Rāghavabhaṭṭa quotes the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā: japa is the repetition of syllables and is loud, whispered or mental. Loud (vācika) japa utters the mantra with high, low and circumflex tones and clear words and syllables; whispered (upāṃśu) japa utters it slowly, the lips moving slightly, barely audible; mental (mānasa) japa recites with the intellect the series of letters, notes and words while remembering the meaning. Loud japa is ten times better than ritual sacrifice, whispered a hundred times, mental a thousand times. Elsewhere: in mental japa one should not move head, neck, tongue or lips.
